Medical History

- Current health concerns and risk factors:
  - Acute worsening of asthma symptoms for 2–3 days: exertional shortness of breath (noted with running and brisk walking), wheeze, cough.
  - Blue inhaler (salbutamol) being used with limited effect.
  - Peak flow when well ~380 L/min (patient-reported). Uses peak flow only intermittently.
  - History of possible eczema/skin issues (patient reports some eczema-like problems).

- Relevant family medical history:

  - Sister: eczema.

  - Clenil (brown inhaler, inhaled corticosteroid preventer) — patient reported using twice daily (patient stated “three puffs twice a day” currently). Advised increase to four puffs twice daily while awaiting review.
  - Cetraben (topical emollient) — dose/route/frequency not documented.

Management Plan

- Immediate actions and advice given:
  - Increase inhaled corticosteroid (Clenil) from reported current 3 puffs twice daily to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting GP review.
  - Continue salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed; may use every 2–4 hours in interim if symptomatic. Advised that frequent use (every 2–4 hours) indicates poorly controlled asthma and is not ideal.
  - If breathing worsens despite interim measures or if unable to be seen in clinic and symptoms deteriorate, attend Emergency Department (A&E) promptly.

- Planned evaluations and possible treatments:
  - Face-to-face GP assessment recommended within the next few days for chest examination and formal peak flow measurement.
  - Depending on clinical findings, possible initiation of oral corticosteroids and/or antibiotics may be required (to be determined at assessment).

- Patient education:
  - Advised about increasing preventer dose temporarily and limits of blue inhaler use; instructed to seek urgent care if condition worsens.

- Follow-up:
  - GP face-to-face review recommended within days (patient to be booked/seen).

  - Preventer inhaler color/name: patient initially described preventer as “blue” when asked, but clinician referred to the brown inhaler Clenil; patient later accepted advice — possible confusion about inhaler names/colors.
